# Governments turn mining data into billions in revenue

[Staff Writer](/external-author?external_author=Staff Writer) | October 12, 2026 | 4:30 am  [Critical Minerals](https://www.mining.com/category/critical-minerals/) [Education](https://www.mining.com/category/education/) [Suppliers & Equipment](https://www.mining.com/category/suppliers-equipment/) [Africa](https://www.mining.com/region/africa/) [Latin America](https://www.mining.com/region/latin-america/) [Cobalt](https://www.mining.com/commodity/cobalt/) [Lithium](https://www.mining.com/commodity/lithium/) [Nickel](https://www.mining.com/commodity/nickel/) [Rare Earth](https://www.mining.com/commodity/rare-earth/)

![Governments are turning mining data into billions of revenue leverage](https://www.mining.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/porgera-mine.png)

The Porgera gold mine is located in the Enga Province of Papua New Guinea. (Image courtesy of [Porgera Joint Venture.](http://www.porgerajv.com/Company/Image-Gallery))

Mining transparency rules are increasingly translating into billions of dollars in protected public revenue, tougher scrutiny of licences and renegotiated resource deals as governments compete for a greater share of mineral wealth, according to [a new global review](https://eiti.org/sites/default/files/EITI%20Impact%20Publication%202026%20EN.pdf?hash=1791367200).

The Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI) said its reporting framework covers 56 countries and about 3,900 entities. Governments have disclosed $3.6 trillion in extractive-sector revenue through the initiative since its establishment in 2003.

The findings show transparency moving beyond the publication of mining payments and into decisions over ownership, licensing, taxation and major project agreements. EITI data has helped governments flag suspect licence applications, scrutinize potentially undervalued transactions and forecast revenue from major mining developments.

The shift is gaining importance as competition for copper, lithium, nickel and other critical minerals accelerates. Resource-rich governments face the challenge of attracting investment while capturing sufficient public revenue and ensuring communities share in the benefits, making access to reliable project and ownership data increasingly important to negotiations and oversight.

## **Revenue leverage**

Some of the clearest financial effects cited by EITI come from Africa, where governments have used disclosed data and financial modelling to reassess major mining agreements.

In the Democratic Republic of Congo, an EITI-commissioned study identified deviations from the [original Sicomines copper-cobalt agreement](https://www.mining.com/web/congo-chinese-partners-sign-reviewed-sicomines-copper-cobalt-joint-venture-agreement/), including unfulfilled infrastructure commitments and changes in profit allocation.

The findings contributed to negotiations that produced a revised agreement in 2024, increasing [planned infrastructure investment to $7 billion](https://www.mining.com/web/congos-7-billion-infrastructure-deal-with-china-will-depend-on-copper-prices/) from $3 billion.

> [Congo’s $7 billion infrastructure deal with China will depend on copper prices](https://www.mining.com/web/congos-7-billion-infrastructure-deal-with-china-will-depend-on-copper-prices/)
